sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. DNA usually appears in the last third of the paper, worth about 6 to 11 marks across a question, opened by a drawing of the molecule: which part is the base [1], name the two substances of the backbone [2], then the base-percentage calculation [3] and, at Higher, the number of amino acids [1]. Summer 2025 ran it as B2 Higher Q10; Summer 2023 asked Foundation candidates for the shape of the molecule and where DNA is found (Q3).
traps: Naming only one of the two backbone substances: in Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q10 most candidates could name one. Learn phosphate and deoxyribose as a pair

The base-percentage chain: in Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q10 quite a few candidates calculated it correctly, and each line carries a mark: double the given base, take that from 100, then halve what is left

Counting the amino acids a length of DNA codes for: Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q10 found it difficult for many. Three bases in a row on one strand code for one amino acid, so count the bases along one strand and divide by three
Not giving the exact name for the shape: in Summer 2023 B2 Foundation Q3 only quite a few candidates wrote double helix
Chromosome numbers in cells other than body cells: Summer 2023 B2 Foundation Q3 records a surprising lack of knowledge of the number in an egg cell and a fertilised egg
Defining the genome: Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q10 notes that the mark went to candidates who had learned the definition, all the genetic material of an organism
Naming the idea that three bases code for one amino acid: many gave base triplet in Summer 2023 B2 Higher Q10; CCEA's schemes refuse 'triple base' and 'triplet base'
The word genome inside a genetic engineering question: only the better candidates gave it in Summer 2023 B2 Higher Q7(a)

steps.decision: Start from the pairing rule, because it is the only fact the question gives you. Every A has a T opposite it, so those two percentages must match.

Because the two strands are the same length
Because a percentage always adds to 100 whatever it describes

workedExamples.stem: A strand of DNA carries the bases A T G C C A. Write the order of the bases on the strand that pairs with it. [3]

steps.working: Write the two rules down first: A with T, C with G.
steps.decision: There are only two pairings, and neither of them ever changes. Writing them at the side stops you guessing halfway along.

steps.working: Work along one base at a time: A → T, T → A, G → C …
steps.decision: One at a time, left to right. Trying to see the whole strand at once is how a base gets missed out.

steps.working: The pairing strand reads T A C G G T.
steps.decision: Check the length: 6 bases in, 6 bases out. A strand that comes out shorter means one was skipped.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: T A C G G T

twin.stem: A strand of DNA carries the bases G C A T. Write the order of the bases on the strand that pairs with it.

workedExamples.stem: In a length of DNA, 24% of the bases are A. Calculate what percentage of the bases are G. Show your working. [3]

steps.working: T = 24%, so A and T together = 48%
steps.decision: A pairs with T, so the two are equal: the pairing rule is the only fact the question gives you.

options: Because every A has a T opposite it
Because A and T are both large bases
Because the four bases are always equal
whyMenu.explain: Each A pairs with one T, so there are exactly as many T bases as A bases.

steps.decision: All four bases make 100%; what the first pair leaves belongs to C and G.
C pairs with G, so they share what is left equally.

twin.stem: In a different length of DNA, 13% of the bases are C. Calculate what percentage are A.

One strand of a short length of DNA reads G C C T A A.
(a) Give the base sequence of its partner strand. [2]
(b) Higher: how many amino acids does this length of DNA code for? [1]

steps.working: G C C T A A pairs with C G G A T T
steps.decision: One base at a time: G with C, C with G, T with A, A with T.

accepted: C G G A T T

any: c g g a t t
c, g, g, a, t, t

steps.working: 6 bases on one strand ÷ 3 = 2 amino acids
steps.decision: The code is read three bases at a time along one strand, so count one strand only.

options: Because each triplet of bases codes for one amino acid
Because each base codes for one amino acid
whyMenu.explain: One triplet, three bases, codes for one amino acid, and only one strand is read.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) C G G A T T. (b) 2.

items.stem: Before we start, three things you have already met. Which part of an animal cell controls its activities and holds its chromosomes?
items.skill: Recall the parts of a cell (B1)

options.feedback: The nucleus. Everything in this topic happens inside it.
The cytoplasm is where most reactions happen, but the chromosomes are not kept there.
The membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.
The mitochondria release energy by respiration.

items.stem: A bacterial cell is different from an animal cell. Which structure does a bacterium NOT have?

options.feedback: No nucleus. Its genetic material lies loose in the cytoplasm instead.
A bacterium does have a cell wall, though not a cellulose one.
Every cell has a membrane.
A bacterium has cytoplasm; that is where its genetic material sits.

items.stem: In a bag of counters, 40% are red and the rest are blue. What percentage are blue?

options.feedback: 100 − 40 = 60. The same move opens every base-percentage question in this topic.
That is the percentage you were given, not the rest.
That would be right only if the two colours were equal, and they are not.
That halves the 40 rather than taking it off 100.

items.stem: What is the genome of an organism?

options.feedback: All of it: every chromosome, every gene, every base.
That is a gene. The genome is the whole set.

options.text: the pair of alleles it carries for one characteristic
options.feedback: That is a genotype for one gene, not the whole genome.
Those are its phenotype. The genome is the material, not the appearance.

items.stem: Two chromosomes of a pair carry the gene for coat colour at the same place. One carries the version for black and the other the version for chestnut. What are those two versions called?
items.skill: Tell a gene from an allele

options.feedback: Alleles: different forms of one gene.
Coat colour is the gene; black and chestnut are its alleles.
A genome is everything, not one version of one gene.
A gamete is a sex cell, not a form of a gene.

items.stem: How many chromosomes are there in the nucleus of a human body cell?

options.feedback: 23 pairs, two in each pair, so 46.
That is the number of pairs, and a gamete's number.
That counts every chromosome of every pair twice.

options.text: it is different in every person
options.feedback: Every human body cell carries the same number. What differs between people is the order of the bases.

items.stem: Which pair of substances forms the backbone of each strand of DNA?

options.feedback: A phosphate and a sugar, deoxyribose, repeating along each strand.
The bases are the rungs across the middle, not part of the backbone.
The sugar is in the backbone but the base is not.
Protein is what the code eventually builds; it is not part of the molecule's backbone.

items.stem: In a length of DNA, which base pairs with C?

options.feedback: C with G, always. The other pair is A with T.
A pairs with T. Pairing C with A would break the rule.
T is A's partner.
A base never pairs with another of the same kind.

items.stem: In a length of DNA, 31% of the bases are G. What percentage are A?
items.skill: Use the pairing rules to find a percentage

options.feedback: G and C take 62%, leaving 38% to share: 19% each.
That is the share for both of the other bases together, before halving.
That subtracts once and stops, as though DNA had only two bases.
The four bases are not present in equal amounts.

items.stem: A strand of DNA carries 24 bases. How many amino acids does it code for?

options.feedback: That counts the bases themselves.
Multiplying by three goes the wrong way.
Halving would mean two bases per amino acid.

(ii) sugar / deoxyribose

parts.workedSolution: (i) is one of the bases, which interlink across the middle. (ii) is the sugar, deoxyribose, and (iii) is a phosphate — together those two make the backbone.

context.setting: Writing the strand that pairs with a given strand

data.caption: One strand of a length of DNA is given. The second row is for the strand that pairs with it.

hints: Only two pairings are possible: A with T, and C with G.
Work along one base at a time rather than trying to see the whole strand at once.

commonErrors.feedback: That copies the first strand instead of pairing with it. Each base must be swapped for its partner: A for T, and C for G.

parts.stem:
The table gives the order of six bases along one strand of a length of DNA.
Complete the second row to show the six bases on the strand that pairs with it.

scheme.for: bases 1 and 2: T and A
bases 3 and 4: C and G
bases 5 and 6: G and T

parts.workedSolution: Take them one at a time. A pairs with T, T pairs with A, G pairs with C, C pairs with G, C pairs with G, A pairs with T. So the second strand reads T A C G G T.

context.setting: Turning one base percentage into another

hints: T only pairs with A, so there is the same percentage of each.
What is left over is shared equally between the other two bases.

commonErrors.feedback: That is what is left for C and G together. They pair with each other, so they share it equally: halve it.
That takes 36% off 100 once. There are four bases, and A takes another 36% before anything is left for C and G.
The four bases are not present in equal amounts. Only T and A match each other; C and G share what is left.
The halving comes at the end, and it is what is LEFT that gets halved, not the percentage you were given.

parts.stem:
In one length of DNA, 36% of the bases are T.
Calculate the percentage of the bases that are C.
Show your working out.

scheme.for: A is the same as T: 36 + 36 = 72

parts.workedSolution: A DNA molecule is built from two long strands. Each strand has a backbone made of a phosphate and a sugar, deoxyribose, repeating along its length, and the bases stick out from that backbone. The bases interlink across the middle in a fixed way: A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. The two strands twist around each other to form a double helix. A chromosome is one long thread of this DNA, held in the nucleus, and in a human body cell the chromosomes lie in functional pairs, 23 pairs in all. A gene is a short length of DNA on a chromosome that controls a characteristic, such as flower colour. An allele is a different form of the same gene, such as the allele for violet flowers and the allele for white flowers. Taken together, all of the genetic material of the organism is its genome.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciara is asked: 'In a length of DNA, 28% of the bases are A. Calculate the percentage of the bases that are C. [3]'
Her working:
studentWorking: A pairs with T, so T is 28% as well
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are exactly right, and they carry two of the three marks. Line 3 hands the whole of the remaining 44% to C. But C pairs with G, so those two must be equal and the 44% is shared between them.
correction: A pairs with T, so T is 28% as well
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks of the three. A quick check catches the rest: add her four percentages up and you get 144, not 100.

findTheMistake.stem:
Oisín is asked: 'A double strand of DNA has 21 base pairs. How many amino acids does it code for? [1]'
His working:
studentWorking: 21 base pairs is 42 bases in all
so it codes for 14 amino acids
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The code is read along one strand only. 21 base pairs means 21 bases on that strand, so line 1 doubles the count, and lines 2 and 3 carry the error on. Summer 2025 examiners found this count difficult for many.
correction: 21 base pairs is 21 bases along one strand
so it codes for 7 amino acids
findTheMistake.feedback: No mark as written: the answer is 7. Divide the number of base pairs by three, never the bases of both strands.
